lead: A color image stores three numbers per pixel instead of one. RGB is the additive model that matches screens: red, green and blue light add to white. HSI describes the same pixel by hue (which color), saturation (how pure) and intensity (how bright), so an algorithm can act on color without being confused by lighting. This chapter covers the RGB cube, 24-bit color, HSI definitions and the conversion formulas. Uses include skin detection in selfies, ripeness sorting of fruit, and traffic-sign detection in driver-assist systems.
prereq: You need: 1.6 for bit depth and quantization, and 1.5 for how a sensor turns light into a pixel value.

sections.h3: RGB: an additive cube of three channels

blocks.text: A color image is three images stacked. Each pixel carries a red value R, a green value G and a blue value B. In an 8-bit color image each channel runs from 0 to 255, so one pixel takes 24 bits. That is 24-bit color: 8 bits per channel, 256 levels per channel, and 256³ = 16,777,216 possible colors per pixel.

RGB is additive; lights add. Red light plus green light looks yellow. The three primaries are red (255,0,0), green (0,255,0) and blue (0,0,255). The secondaries are the pairwise sums: yellow (255,255,0), magenta (255,0,255) and cyan (0,255,255). All channels at maximum give white (255,255,255); all at zero give black (0,0,0). Equal values in all three channels, R = G = B, give a gray level.
Put R, G and B on three perpendicular axes and every pixel sits inside a cube of side 255 — the RGB color cube. The diagonal from black to white is the gray axis.

RGB is device-friendly, not perception-friendly. Camera sensors, phone screens and JPEG files speak RGB, so that is where images arrive. But the numbers do not match what you see: distance inside the cube does not track how different two colors look, and a change of lighting moves all three numbers at once.
HSI describes a pixel the way a person does: what color is it, how pure is it, how bright is it.

items: Hue H: which color, an angle from 0° to 360° around a color wheel. Red sits at 0°, green at 120°, blue at 240°. Hue says nothing about brightness.
Saturation S: how far the color is from gray, from 0 to 1. S = 0 means gray or white; S = 1 means a fully pure color. Mixing white paint into red lowers S and leaves the hue red.
Intensity I: brightness, from 0 (black) up to the maximum level. It is the average of the three channels, not the largest channel.

blocks.text: Switch on a lamp and the pixel gets brighter — I moves, H stays roughly put. A shadow dims the pixel — again mostly I. So a threshold on H and S copes with lighting changes that would break the same threshold in RGB. Skin detection, fruit ripeness grading and traffic-sign detection often convert to HSI for this reason.
HSV, also called HSB, is a close relative: its brightness term V is max(R,G,B), not the average, so the two models give different numbers for the same pixel.

sections.h3: Converting RGB to HSI, and what color processing means

blocks.text: Three formulas do the conversion. Keep R, G and B on one scale — 0 to 1, or 0 to 255. The ratio and difference forms cancel a common scale, but a pixel written with mixed scales gives a wrong hue.

blocks.where: R, G, B are the channel values on one common scale; I is intensity on that same scale.
min(R,G,B) is the smallest of the three channel values; S is saturation, in [0, 1]; if R = G = B = 0 the pixel is black and S is defined as 0.

blocks.text: H = 60°·(G − B)/(max − min) if max = R;  H = 60°·[2 + (B − R)/(max − min)] if max = G;  H = 60°·[4 + (R − G)/(max − min)] if max = B
blocks.where: max and min are the largest and smallest of R, G and B; H is hue in degrees, in [0°, 360°); add 360° to a negative result; if max = min the pixel is gray, hue is undefined and by convention H = 0°.

items: Take the three channel values of the pixel on one common scale.
Find max, min and the sum R + G + B.
Compute I as the sum divided by 3.
Compute S from the ratio of min to the sum; use S = 0 when the sum is 0.
Pick the hue case by which channel equals max, and evaluate it.
If H came out negative, add 360° to bring it into [0°, 360°).

blocks.text: When two channels tie at the maximum, the cases agree at that boundary.

Two names cover the work. Pseudo-color processing maps a single-channel gray image to colors for display only — intensity slicing of a thermal or X-ray image adds no new measurement. Full-color processing works on the three channels of a real color image. Running the same gray-level operation on R, G and B separately is cheap and correct for geometry and smoothing, but per-channel histogram equalization changes the three channels by different amounts and tints a plain gray wall. The fix is to convert to HSI, change I alone, and convert back with H and S untouched.
Color enhancement and filtering are taken up in Unit 2, color segmentation in Unit 4, and calibration and color constancy in Unit 5.

examples.question: An 8-bit color pixel has RGB = (255, 128, 0). Convert it to HSI. Give H in degrees to one decimal place, S to two decimals, and I on the 0–255 scale.
steps: max = 255 (the red channel), min = 0 (the blue channel), sum = 255 + 128 + 0 = 383.
S = 1 − 3 × 0 / 383 = 1 − 0 = 1.0, so the color is fully saturated.
max = R, so use the red case: H = 60° × (G − B) / (max − min) = 60° × (128 − 0) / 255.
H is positive, so no 360° correction is needed.
examples.answer: H ≈ 30.1°, S = 1.0 and I ≈ 127.67, a fully saturated orange.
examples.check:
R, G, B = 255, 128, 0
mx, mn = max(R, G, B), min(R, G, B)
I = (R + G + B) / 3
S = 1 - 3 * mn / (R + G + B)
H = 60 * (G - B) / (mx - mn)   # max is R, so the red case
print(round(I, 2))
print(round(S, 2))
print(round(H, 1))

traps: I is the average of the three channels, not the maximum. Writing I = max(R,G,B) is the V of HSV, not I of HSI; the two models give different numbers for the same pixel.
Hue is an angle. Hues 350° and 10° are 20° apart, crossing 0°, not 340° apart.
The hue formulas need a scale-consistent max − min. Mixing 0–1 and 0–255 values inside one pixel gives a wrong hue.
For a black pixel R = G = B = 0 the saturation term becomes 0/0. State S = 0, H = 0 and do not divide.
24-bit color means 8 bits per channel, not 24 levels per channel. Three channels at 8 bits give 256³ ≈ 16.8 million colors.

quiz.q: How many bits does one pixel take in 24-bit RGB, and how are they split?
quiz.a: 24 bits, split as 8 bits per channel, so 256 levels for each of R, G and B.

quiz.q: Name the three secondary colors of RGB and give their (R,G,B) triples at full level.
Why does an HSI-based threshold survive a change of lighting better than an RGB-based one?
quiz.a: A change of illumination moves mainly the intensity I, while hue H and saturation S stay close to their old values. A threshold on H therefore keeps selecting the same color, whereas all three RGB values shift together.

quiz.q: State one difference between HSV and HSI.
quiz.a: In HSV the brightness term is V = max(R,G,B); in HSI the brightness term is the average I = (R+G+B)/3. The hue formulas are otherwise the same.

quiz.q: Convert RGB = (0, 128, 255) (8-bit) to HSI. Give H in degrees to one decimal place, S to two decimals, and I on the 0–255 scale.
A pixel has R = G = B = 90. Give H, S and I on the 0–255 scale.
quiz.a: max = min = 90, so the pixel is gray and H is undefined, taken as 0°. I = 270/3 = 90. S = 1 − 3×90/270 = 1 − 1 = 0.

quiz.q: Compare the HSI values of (255,0,0) and (255,60,60). What changed and what did not?
quiz.a: For (255,0,0): max = 255, min = 0, I = 85, S = 1.0, H = 0°. For (255,60,60): max = 255, min = 60, sum = 375, I = 125, S = 1 − 180/375 = 0.52, H = 60°×(60−60)/255 = 0°. The hue is unchanged at 0° (still red) and saturation has dropped from 1.0 to 0.52, so the second pixel is a washed-out pink; intensity also rose from 85 to 125.

quiz.q: Histogram equalization applied separately to R, G and B gives a gray wall a green tint. Explain why, and give the HSI fix.
quiz.a: The three channel histograms differ, so equalization applies a different mapping to each channel. Three equal input values no longer come out equal, and unequal channels mean a color where there was gray. The fix: convert to HSI, equalize I only, and convert back keeping H and S unchanged, so gray pixels stay gray.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real pipelines rarely stop at HSI. JPEG and video codecs convert RGB to YCbCr and store color detail at lower resolution, because the eye is less sensitive to color detail than to brightness. Displays assume sRGB, a gamma-encoded RGB, so arithmetic that models light must first decode the gamma. Perceptual spaces such as CIELAB make equal numeric distance look like equal visual distance. Search next: sRGB gamma, YCbCr 4:2:0, CIELAB ΔE, color constancy.
